title: NY State Assembly · District 83
area: Northeast Bronx, including Edenwald, Wakefield, Williamsbridge, Baychester and Co-op City.

context.text: Incumbent Carl Heastie, Speaker of the New York State Assembly since February 2015, is unopposed in the Democratic primary. James Washington-Ward, who ran unsuccessfully for New York City Council District 12 in 2025 on the Conservative and United Alliance Party lines (2.8% of the vote), is the Conservative Party nominee for this seat; his Republican primary bid was withdrawn or disqualified, and he advanced on the Conservative line only.

candidates.name: Carl Heastie
candidates.currentRole: Speaker of the New York State Assembly; Assembly Member, District 83 (since 2001)

summary.text: Carl Heastie is the Democratic nominee for re-election in NY Assembly District 83 in the northeast Bronx. A former finance manager and New York City Comptroller's office budget analyst, he was first elected to the Assembly in 2000, chaired the Assembly Labor Committee, and has been Speaker since February 3, 2015, the first African American to lead the chamber.

background.text: Earned a B.S. in applied mathematics and statistics from SUNY Stony Brook and an MBA from Baruch College (CUNY). The Assembly bio says he is a product of New York City's public schools.
Worked as a finance manager, an account manager and a budget analyst, beginning his career as a budget analyst in the New York City Comptroller's office, before joining the Assembly.

Has been a member of the Democratic State Committee since 1996 and chaired the Bronx Democratic Party's county elections committee from 1992 to 2000. Ballotpedia lists him as chair of the Bronx Democratic County Committee from 2008 to 2015.
Was first elected to the Assembly in 2000 to represent the 83rd District in the northeast Bronx, winning the general election with 93% of the vote, and took office in 2001.

Chaired the Assembly Labor Committee (2013 to 2015, per Ballotpedia) before becoming Speaker. His Assembly biography says he was the principal negotiator of a minimum-wage increase, enacted in 2016 as a graduated plan to raise the statewide minimum wage, and that before becoming Speaker he was prime sponsor of the Wage Theft Prevention Act.

According to his Assembly biography, before becoming Speaker he championed a law prohibiting the sale of water containing nicotine to people under 18 and authored a law releasing domestic-violence victims from lease obligations when remaining in the residence would endanger them.
Elected the 100th Speaker of the New York State Assembly on February 3, 2015, the first African American to lead the 150-member chamber.
His Assembly biography says he was instrumental in efforts that led to the 2016 announcement of a new YMCA facility in the Edenwald neighborhood of the Bronx.

priorities.text: Criminal justice reform: continuing to build on the elimination of cash bail for most misdemeanor and non-violent felony offenses, speedy-trial and discovery reforms, and raising the age of criminal responsibility to 18.

Affordable housing: building on the Housing Stability and Tenant Protection Act of 2019, which made the state's tenant protections permanent and limited rent increases, retaliatory eviction and security deposits.
Investing in education, including boosting state school aid and easing the cost of higher education.
Protecting the environment and combating climate change, building on the Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act.
Combating gun violence through further commonsense gun-safety measures.

positions.summary: Negotiated and passed the Housing Stability and Tenant Protection Act of 2019, which made the state's rent regulations permanent, eliminated the vacancy bonus, limited rent increases for major capital improvements, and banned lease application fees.
Negotiated and passed the 2019 Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act, which set goals of cutting greenhouse gas emissions 85% by 2050 and reaching emissions-free electricity by 2040.

Passed a package of gun-safety laws including the Red Flag law, which lets courts issue risk protection orders to keep firearms from people found to pose a danger to themselves or others, a ban on bump stocks, expanded background-check requirements, and a 2018 law barring people convicted of domestic-violence crimes from purchasing or possessing firearms.
Negotiated the dedicated MTA funding source in the 2019-20 state budget that established congestion pricing in Manhattan, the first such program in a U.S. city.
As Assembly Labor Committee chair and later Speaker, was the principal negotiator of increases to the statewide minimum wage, including the 2016 law enacting a graduated $15 minimum wage.

record.text: As Speaker, negotiated and passed the SFY 2019-20 budget, which eliminated cash bail for most misdemeanor and non-violent felony offenses and reformed the discovery process.
Led passage of the Humane Alternatives to Long-Term (HALT) Solitary Confinement Act, restricting solitary confinement in New York prisons and jails.
Led passage of the Marijuana Regulation and Taxation Act (MRTA), legalizing adult-use marijuana in New York.
Negotiated and passed the Housing Stability and Tenant Protection Act of 2019, a statewide package of tenant protections.
Negotiated the dedicated MTA funding source in the SFY 2019-20 budget that established congestion pricing in Manhattan.
Negotiated and passed the Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act.
Passed a package of gun-safety measures including the Red Flag law, a bump-stock ban, and expanded background-check requirements.

Sponsored A.11726, the Wage Theft Prevention Act, which established notice requirements for employees in their primary languages and protections for workers reclaiming withheld wages; signed into law by Gov. David Paterson on December 13, 2010.
As Assembly Labor Committee chair, was the principal negotiator of the 2016 law enacting a graduated statewide minimum-wage increase toward $15.
Elected the 100th Speaker of the New York State Assembly, the first African American to lead the chamber.

candidates.name: James Washington-Ward

summary.text: James Washington-Ward is the Conservative Party nominee for NY Assembly District 83 and the party's district leader for the 83rd Assembly District. Born and raised in the Bronx, he ran for New York City Council District 12 in 2025 on the Conservative and United Alliance Party lines, finishing third with 2.8% of the vote. He has not held elected office.

background.text: Born and raised in the Bronx; briefly lived in Pennsylvania before returning, and lives in the Baychester neighborhood. Graduated from Samuel Gompers Vocational Technical High School and was a member of the Star of the Sea Sea Cadet Corps, a Bronx youth organization.

Was serving as the Conservative Party District Leader for the 83rd Assembly District as of December 2024, when a local news profile described his first campaign, for New York City Council District 12, and said it centered on police-community relations and youth and community programs.

Ran for New York City Council District 12 in the November 4, 2025 general election on the Conservative and United Alliance Party lines, finishing third behind incumbent Kevin Riley (D) and Franchie Muniz Sr. (R) with 873 votes (2.8%).
Was endorsed by the Bronx Conservative Party as its 2026 candidate for State Assembly District 83.

candidates.researchNotes: No campaign website, Ballotpedia Candidate Connection survey response, or policy statements specific to this Assembly race could be located for Washington-Ward. Background is drawn from a Big Apple Gazette profile published during his 2025 City Council campaign and a Bronx.com report on the Bronx Conservative Party's 2026 endorsement meeting; neither addresses state-legislative issues, so no priorities or positions are documented.

researchNotes: Heastie's record draws on his official Assembly biography and his campaign issues pages, which describe his role as Speaker in negotiating and passing statewide legislation rather than individual bill sponsorships (Speakers rarely sponsor bills themselves); one specific sponsored bill (the 2010 Wage Theft Prevention Act, from before he became Speaker) is documented on Ballotpedia. Neither candidate completed a 2026 Ballotpedia Candidate Connection survey. Washington-Ward has no campaign website or Assembly-specific policy statements; his entry adds biography from local news coverage of his 2025 City Council run and his 2026 Bronx Conservative Party endorsement.
